title: 3-Read Friday #111: Practice, Belonging, and Predicting Student Errors
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #111 presents three blog posts on mathematics education and cognitive science selected for their practical and theoretical value. The first, by Dylan Kane, argues that procedural mathematical skills should be practiced in short, spaced chunks across multiple days guided by daily comprehension checks, because durable learning requires building storage strength rather than optimizing for single-lesson performance. The second, by Jon Hutchinson, reframes belonging not as a soft moral goal but as a cognitive prerequisite: students uncertain about belonging spend working memory on social vigilance, directly reducing the cognitive bandwidth available for the lesson's content. The third, by Colin Foster and Aidan Stannard using Barton's own Diagnostic Questions platform, shows that secondary mathematics teachers can rapidly sharpen error-prediction accuracy through short repeated prediction cycles against real student data -- a low-cost, high-leverage professional development intervention. Barton's editorial voice connects each post's central empirical claim to practical classroom implications.
points: Dylan Kane's retrieval-practice framework: procedural mathematics skills should be practiced in short, spaced chunks across multiple days with daily comprehension checks, because durable learning depends on building storage strength -- not on single-lesson performance optimization.

Jon Hutchinson's belonging-as-cognitive-prerequisite argument: social uncertainty consumes working memory that should be available for the content being taught, making belonging a direct enabler of cognitive engagement rather than a nice-to-have social outcome.

Foster and Stannard's diagnostic-data cycles finding: secondary mathematics teachers can rapidly sharpen their ability to predict which student errors will occur -- and in what proportions -- through short prediction cycles against Diagnostic Questions data, representing a promising low-cost route to Pedagogical Content Knowledge.

All three posts share a common theme: teacher expertise grown through close attention to real student responses and deliberate feedback loops outperforms generic professional development that operates at a distance from actual classroom data.
quotes: As much as I love research into retrieval practise, nothing beats reading about how an actual teacher is using it day to day with their students.

Dylan argues that procedural skills in maths should be practised in short, spaced chunks across multiple days -- guided by daily checks for understanding -- until students can reliably retrieve them, because durable learning depends on building storage strength, not just performance within a single lesson.

Powerful stuff from Jon here. He argues that belonging is best understood not as a soft moral goal but as a cognitive one -- pupils who are uncertain whether they belong spend working memory on social vigilance that should be available for learning, so building belonging directly expands the cognitive bandwidth available for the content we teach.
Okay, a bit of a self-indulgent selection to end this week, as it involves my Diagnostic Questions website, but I hope you'll forgive me because it's fascinating.

Colin and Aidan show that secondary maths teachers can rapidly sharpen their ability to predict which errors students will make -- and in what proportions -- through short, repeated cycles of prediction against diagnostic question data, making this a promising, low-cost route to developing a critical strand of Pedagogical Content Knowledge.
